newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: G7 envoys express concern to Cambodia's Hun Sen.
newsitem.headline: G7 envoys express concern to Cambodia's Hun Sen.

text.p: Two special envoys from the Group of Seven industrial countries met Cambodia's Second Prime Minister Hun Sen on Thursday and told him of group's concern about political stability in Cambodia, a Japanese official said.

Claude Martin, the French Foreign Ministry's Deputy Secretary General, and Yukio Imagawa, a former Japanese ambassador in Phnom Penh, met Hun Sen for more than two and a half hours at his Phnom Penh residence.
"We reported to the prime minister. The message is clear. It is the statement of the G8," Shohei Naito, Japan's Ambassador to Cambodia, who took part in the talks, told reporters after the meeting.
The envoys, who did not talk to reporters, were scheduled to meet First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh later on Thursday.

The G7 leaders, who met with Russian President Boris Yeltsin in Denver last weekend, called for an end to the political chaos and violence in Cambodia that they said threatened to shatter the relative stability since United Nations-sponsored elections in 1993.
At the end of their summit the G7 urged Cambodia's fractious leaders to "demonstrate their commitment to holding free and fair elections by setting a specific date".
Ranariddh announced on Tuesday that he and Hun Sen, partners in an uneasy coalition, had agreed that Cambodia's next general election will be in May.
"He told the two envoys about the general situation in Cambodia and about the decision of both prime ministers on the election," Hun Sen's spokesman, Om Yentieng, told reporters after the talks.
The envoys arrived as political tension remained high in Cambodia due to a long-running feud between the two prime ministers over the division of power in their rocky coalition.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright announced earlier that she was cancelling a trip to Cambodia because of security concerns.
Ranariddh's royalist party won the 1993 election but agreed to form the coalition with Hun Sen after he objected to the election results.
Hun Sen led the communist government which ruled the country prior to the U.N.-organised peace process.
Relations between the two premiers turned icy last year after Ranariddh demanded that he be given a greater share of power to govern in the provinces.
Their dispute has deadlocked government. The national assembly was unable to reconvene in April as scheduled, preventing the passing of key legislation, including electoral laws.
Last week bodyguards loyal to the two prime ministers fought a gun battle on the streets of the capital which left two of Ranariddh's men dead.
Hun Sen told the G7 envoys that the main stumbling block was the deadlocked national assembly and problems would be resolved once the parliament reconvened.
"We must join together to hold a meeting of the national assembly to pass the electoral laws and other laws," Om Yentieng quoted Hun Sen as telling the envoys.
The disintegrating Khmer Rouge guerrilla force has inflamed the two premiers' feud with both men seeking to make political capital as the group breaks apart.
